# The Homework That Never Was

I stood at the front of Mrs. Patterson's classroom, my hands trembling slightly as I delivered the classic line every teacher has heard a thousand times before: "My dog ate my homework." I held up the evidence—a crumpled, saliva-soaked wad of paper that I'd hastily chewed on that morning to make the story believable.

Mrs. Patterson raised one eyebrow, clearly unconvinced. "Is that so?" she asked, crossing her arms.

Sensing her doubt, I panicked and did what any reasonable person would do: I made things worse. Much worse.

"Well, actually," I stammered, "it's a bit more complicated than that. You see, my dog didn't just *eat* my homework. He *cooked* it first."

The classroom fell silent. Mrs. Patterson's eyebrow climbed even higher.

"Cooked it?" she repeated slowly.

"Yes!" I continued, my imagination now running wild with no brakes in sight. "He turned my math worksheet into a delicious lasagna, layering the pages like pasta sheets. Then he took my history essay and turned it into a stir-fry, and my spelling list became a garnish for the whole dish."

I could see the disbelief spreading across her face, but instead of stopping, I doubled down. "He was wearing this little chef's apron—red and white checkered pattern—and this tall white chef's hat. He even seasoned everything with ketchup and mustard because apparently my dog has *very* specific culinary preferences."

"Your dog," Mrs. Patterson said flatly, "wore an apron and a chef's hat, and seasoned your homework with condiments."

"And he was humming while he cooked," I added, digging myself deeper into a hole with no bottom in sight. "Some kind of Italian opera, I think. He's very passionate about his cooking."

By this point, Mrs. Patterson had reached her limit. She pinched the bridge of her nose, took a deep breath, and pointed toward the door. "Office. Now."

As I trudged down the hallway toward the principal's office, replaying the ridiculous tale I'd just spun, I couldn't help but feel a pang of guilt. Not because I'd been caught in an increasingly absurd lie about a talking, singing, gourmet-cooking dog—but because of one small, glaring problem with my entire story.

I didn't actually own a dog.

I had a cat. And the truth was far less creative than my elaborate culinary fantasy: my homework had been shredded into confetti-like pieces by my cat, who had decided my math worksheet made an excellent scratching post the night before. There was no apron, no chef's hat, no ketchup-seasoned lasagna—just a very smug feline sitting in the wreckage of my assignment, looking thoroughly unbothered by the chaos she'd caused.

Sitting outside the principal's office, I sighed and accepted my fate. Sometimes the truth is far less interesting than the lie, but at least the truth doesn't get you sent to the office for insisting your pet moonlights as a five-star chef.

# The Homework Incident

Mr. Peterson stood at the front of the classroom, his eyebrows raised in that particular way that meant trouble. "Marcus, I don't see your essay on my desk."

Marcus Chen felt his stomach drop. He hadn't done the assignment—he'd been playing video games all weekend—and now, staring into his teacher's stern face, the truth felt impossible to say out loud.

"It's... it's a really weird story, Mr. Peterson."

"Try me."

"My dog ate it."

Mr. Peterson's eyes narrowed. "Your dog."

"Yes. But—it's not a normal dog situation. See, my dog, Biscuit, he's... he's a chef. Like, a really good one. He was making beef wellington last night, and he needed parchment paper, and my essay was the closest paper-like thing, so he just... used it. As parchment paper. For the wellington."

The class snickered. Mr. Peterson's expression didn't change. "Your dog cooks."

"He's very talented," Marcus said, warming to the story despite himself. "He went to culinary school. Well, not *went*—he watched a lot of cooking shows and sort of absorbed the knowledge."

"Marcus."

"He can also talk," Marcus blurted, unable to stop himself now that he'd started. "Just a little. Mostly about food. He said 'more salt' once. Clear as day."

A few kids were outright laughing now. Mr. Peterson crossed his arms.

"So let me get this straight. Your talking, cooking dog ate your homework because he mistook it for parchment paper while preparing a beef wellington."

"When you say it like that it sounds unbelievable, but—yes."

"And where is Biscuit now?"

"Recovering. From the stress of the kitchen. He works long hours."

Mr. Peterson pinched the bridge of his nose. "Marcus, does this dog have a name tag? A vet? Any evidence he exists beyond this story you're spinning worse by the second?"

Sensing the story was collapsing, Marcus doubled down instead of retreating. "He's actually won awards. Small, local awards. From a dog cooking competition. It's a niche community, you wouldn't have heard of it."

"A dog cooking competition."

"For talking dogs specifically. It's very exclusive."

The classroom was in near-chaos now, kids doubled over laughing, and Mr. Peterson had clearly reached his limit. "Office. Now."

Marcus trudged down the hallway toward the principal's office, his elaborate tale unraveling behind him with every step. By the time he sat down across from Principal Alvarez, the absurdity of what he'd said had fully caught up with him.

"So," Principal Alvarez said, reading the incident slip Mr. Peterson had sent along. "A talking dog. Who cooks. Who ate your homework as parchment paper for a beef wellington. And has *won awards*."

Marcus slumped in his chair. "It sounded better in my head."

"I'm sure it did." She set the paper down. "Marcus, do you even have a dog?"

There was a long pause.

"No," Marcus admitted quietly. "I have a cat."

Principal Alvarez blinked. "A cat."

"Yeah. Her name's Pretzel. She actually did eat my homework, though. Or—chewed it up and threw up on it, more accurately. It's disgusting and it's in a bag in my backpack right now, if you want proof."

The principal stared at him for a long moment, torn between exasperation and disbelief. "Let me get this straight. You invented an entire fictional talking, cooking, award-winning dog... when the truth was just a cat throwing up on your homework?"

Marcus shrugged helplessly. "I panicked."

"You had actual evidence the whole time?"

"It's really gross evidence. I didn't want to bring it up."

Principal Alvarez sighed, rubbing her temples, caught somewhere between wanting to laugh and wanting to send him straight back to detention. "Next time, Marcus, just lead with the disgusting cat evidence. It'll save us all a lot of time."

# Before, And, But: The Architecture of Change

Every story we tell ourselves is built from three simple words that shape how we understand our lives.

**Before** is where we begin. It's the version of ourselves that existed prior to knowledge, prior to loss, prior to love. Before is innocent in a sense—not ignorant, but unshaped by whatever comes next. We often don't recognize a "before" until it's already over. It's only in hindsight that we say, "Before I met her, I didn't understand what mattered," or "Before that diagnosis, I took my health for granted." Before is the calm we don't notice until the storm arrives.

**And** is continuation. It's the word of accumulation, of one thing building upon another without contradiction. And says: this happened, and then this happened, and then this. It's the rhythm of ordinary life—steady, additive, moving forward without resistance. And doesn't ask us to reconsider anything; it simply says there's more. More days, more experiences, more evidence for the story we're already telling. And is comfortable. And is safe. And, if we're not careful, and can become the only word we ever use—stringing together moments without ever stopping to ask if the story itself needs to change.

**But** is the rupture. It's the word that interrupts the momentum of and and forces a reckoning. But says: everything I just told you—reconsider it. But is uncomfortable because it demands complexity. "I loved my job, but something was missing." "I thought I knew him, but I was wrong." But doesn't erase what came before; it complicates it, adds shadow and depth, forces us to hold two truths simultaneously.

Together, these three words trace the shape of transformation. We live in a *before*, we string together *ands* until we've built a life, and then a single *but* arrives—unbidden, often unwelcome—and everything shifts. The genius of human resilience isn't in avoiding the *but*; it's in what we do after it. Do we return to simple *ands*, pretending the interruption never happened? Or do we let the *but* become a new *before*, the start of a story we haven't yet finished telling?

Perhaps growth is just this: learning to welcome the word that ruins our sentences, because it's often the only word honest enough to tell the truth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a funny rhyming poem about a kid making up an outlandish excuse to their teacher for not doing their homework.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Homework Catastrophe

Dear Mrs. Peterson, I know I'm late,
But listen close, this tale is great!
Last night at eight, while doing math,
A dragon crashed right through my bath!

He wasn't mean, just kind of rude,
He saw my homework and thought: "Food!"
He gobbled up my worksheet fast,
Said "Fractions, yum!" and then he gassed
The room with smoke that smelled like cheese,
While I just stood there, weak in knees.

Then Grandma's parrot joined the fun,
Snatched my pencil and made a run!
He flew in circles round my head,
Screaming "Polly wants math instead!"
I chased that bird through every room,
Armed only with a kitchen broom.

Meanwhile my goldfish, Mr. Bubbles,
Escaped his bowl and caused more troubles—
He grew some legs (I don't know how!)
And started doing long division now,
But then he sneezed (fish sneeze, it's true)
And turned my answers into goo.

My little brother, dressed as Thor,
Declared my homework "needs some more
Excitement, drama, superpowers!"
He hammered it for forty hours.
By then the dragon wanted seconds,
The parrot still to math had beckoned,

The goldfish grew a tiny beard,
And honestly, it all got weird.

So here I stand with empty hands,
No homework left—you understand?
I could've fought through all that chaos,
But dragons plus math? Total no-go zone.

So Mrs. Peterson, please don't fuss,
I'll redo it—no need to cuss.
Just keep the dragons, birds, and fish
Away from my homework wish.

*The teacher sighed, then start to grin,*
*"Detention, kid. But nice one. Come on in."*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a humorous children's poem in the style of Shel Silverstein about a dog that "ate" someone's homework?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Homework Hound

I know you've heard this story
told a thousand times before,
"My dog ate all my homework!"
(said by kids from door to door)

But mine's a different story,
so please just hear me out—
my dog did NOT eat homework,
of that there is no doubt!

He ate my calculator,
he ate my pencil case,
He ate the goldfish crackers
that I dropped upon my face.

He ate my little sister's shoe,
he ate the TV remote,
He even ate a button
off my brand new winter coat.

He ate the mail, he ate a chair,
he ate my mother's hat,
He ate a slice of pizza
and then threw up on the mat.

But here's the twist you didn't see,
the part that's really true—
He ate so much of *everything*
that homework's missing too!

It's somewhere in his belly
with the buttons and the shoe,
So really, Teacher, isn't it
technically true?

I didn't lose my homework,
I didn't make an excuse,
That dog's a garbage disposal
who's simply on the loose!

So if you'd like the homework back,
I know just what to do—
Just wait a day or two
and I'll bring it back... to you.

Though honestly I'd rather
just do it all again,
Than wait around for THAT
to come out the other end!
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a silly narrative poem with a twist ending where the excuse for missing homework spirals out of control.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Excuse That Ate the Classroom**

Little Jasper Pruitt-Snoot forgot his homework Tuesday,
and when the teacher asked him why, he said, "It's kind of a whole day."

"My dog," he said, "he ate it—" but then paused and shook his head,
"Actually, that's boring. Here's the truth instead:

My dog *did* eat my homework, but the paper made him strange,
he grew three extra legs and then began to rearrange

the furniture in alphabetic piles across the yard,
and honestly, Miss Fenwick, the transformation was quite hard

to watch, because he started glowing, speaking fluent French,
and hosting a small dinner party for a startled garden wrench."

The teacher raised one eyebrow. "Jasper, that's a lot."
"Oh, it gets much bigger," Jasper said. "That's really not the plot—

because the wrench, it turns out, was a wizard in disguise,
who'd been trapped in metal form since 1855,

and when he broke the curse he was so grateful and so glad
he multiplied my homework into *every sheet I'd had*,

then the sheets turned into pigeons, and the pigeons formed a choir,
and they sang the missing digits of the value known as pi,

which summoned forth a portal shaped exactly like our school,
which sucked in half the playground and reversed the swimming pool,

and *that's* when things got tricky, because Principal Malone
got turned into a gumball machine and started eating stone,

and honestly from there it's mostly explosions, myths, and lore,
a kraken, then a wedding, then a minor dinosaur—

but the POINT is, Miss, my homework simply couldn't be replaced
once it had reorganized the fabric of time and space."

Silence held the classroom. Chalk dust drifted, softly stilled.
Miss Fenwick blinked, then calmly said, "Alright. Extension's filled.

But one more thing, before you sit—" she smiled, serene, polite—
"I'll need you to explain this to the school board, Thursday night,

because the janitor reported seeing pigeons in the hall,
and Principal Malone's been oddly *shiny* since the fall,

and there's a kraken tentacle stuck in the vending machine,
and half the playground's missing, and the pool's gone... kind of green."

Jasper's face went pale. He hadn't meant a word of it—
he'd made it up entirely, hadn't thought he'd made a hit—

but sure enough, that Thursday, there in front of the school board,
sat a gumball-shaped Malone and one bewildered, singing bird.

Moral of this story, kids, in case you didn't glean:
be careful what you fib about—it just might intervene.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

# The Great Homework Catastrophe

"You're late again," my teacher said,
"And where's your homework, Fred?"
I gulped and stared down at my shoe,
"Well, funny story... it's kinda through."

"My dog, you see, he's quite the chef,
Trained himself—I'm not deaf!
He took my math sheet off the table,
Said 'Woof!' which means 'I'm able!'"

"He preheated the oven to 350 degrees,
Grabbed some oven mitts with ease,
Sprinkled cheese across my essay,
(He's French-inspired, very fancy!)"

"He folded fractions into thirds,
Garnished spelling words with herbs,
Basted my book report in gravy,
Then declared, 'This dish is TASTY!'"

"He used a whisk to beat the numbers,
Let my science notes simmer under
A low flame for twenty minutes,
Added paprika—he's got spirit!"

"He plated it all so elegant-like,
Called it his 'Homework à la Spike,'
Lit a candle, poured some water,
(In my bowl, not like he oughta)"

"He took a bite and gave a nod,
'Magnifique!' he said—how odd!
Then he ate the WHOLE thing, front to back,
Even licked the plate—yes, that's a fact!"

My teacher blinked, then crossed her arms,
Unimpressed by doggy charms.
"That's the wildest thing I've heard.
Sit down, Fred—that's quite absurd."

"But here's the deal, you clever creature:
Next time, feed the dog to your teacher—
I mean, just DO the homework, please,
Save the recipes for cheese!"

counterfactuals.output:
# The Legend of Rex

My dog is huge, my dog is fierce,
He's got a bark that'll pierce your ears,
He chased a mailman down the street,
And ate a burglar's stinky feet!

He wrestled bears when he was two,
He howled at the moon and scared it blue,
He's strong enough to pull a truck,
And once outran a speeding duck!

My dog can leap ten stories high,
He's basically learned to fly,
He guards our house both day and night,
And never loses any fight!

So teacher, that's my essay done,
About my dog who's second to none,
His name is Rex, he's my best friend—

"Wait, isn't that your cat, Ben?"

I paused, my confidence deflated,
"Well... technically, that's overstated.
Rex is fluffy, Rex is small,
Rex is only two feet tall.

He does sleep twenty hours a day,
And bats at yarn balls when he plays,
That 'burglar' was a toy mouse, true,
And 'bears' were just my socks—round two.

The mailman thing? He hissed one time.
The moon thing? Also just a rhyme.
But he *did* jump on the fridge last week!"

The class erupted—Ben just shrieked,

"That's MY cat, you weirdo, Fred!
You've been writing about HIM instead?!"
I shrugged and grinned, "Same difference, dude—
A legend's just... exaggerated food."
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
